26855-hard-guy:
H. B. Carleton set this short tale in the year 2000, when streamlined automobiles run themselves down glassite super-highways at ninety miles an hour. Frederick Marden, a salesman, would usually pass a hitch-hiker by, but this one's bearing makes him brake. The man slides in with casual deliberateness, speaks from the corner of his mouth, and names Dentonville, the next town, as his goal. His celo-lex clothing is rather ragged, and his steady blue eyes show no emotion.

The passenger calls himself Mike Eagen, head of the Strato Rovers, the toughest mob this side of Mars. They spare honest people, he says, but take theirs from crooks and racketeers who cannot squeal to the Interplanetary Police. A mystery ray paralyzes anyone who starts up with them. Marden, who owns only an old heap, learns that picking up a hitch-hiker is still as dangerous as ever.
27161-our-guy:
Mrs. E. E. Boyd's Our Guy, or The Elder Brother, published in Boston in 1875, follows Guy through a year of family and faith. Chapters open on New Year's Eve, weigh Guy or Christ, and introduce little Philip, before death, then life, and Guy giving his views in full.

Later chapters bring the Young People's Association, a day of pleasure, Miss Smithers and a surprise, and Pete's slavery and freedom. A deathbed scene, with hands raised and clasped and a nurse urging prayer, anchors the book's earnest evangelical portrait of an elder brother.
75766-letters-to-guy:
Letters to Guy, by Lady Barker, was published in London in 1885. Macmillan issued the book of travel letters. Barker had written Station Life in New Zealand. Guy is her boy, left behind, and the letters run home to him. Letter one is dated at Adelaide in May 1883. It is her first chance to write since leaving Mauritius a fortnight before. The cold struck the party hard after Mauritian sun. Her son Louis soon helped the sailors at every turn. He learned the French words for the ship's speed, and the log was never heaved without him.

A pug puppy, Monsieur Puppy, knew only French as yet. The valet Rosidore wrapped himself like a wool-bale by the funnel. The big French steamer ploughed south-east through rough seas toward Australia. Barker writes a mother's shipboard diary in letter form.
britannica-1911-crequy:
Créquy is the name of a French noble family from Picardy. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its line back to the tenth century. It took its name from a small lordship in Pas de Calais. Great houses sprang from it: Blécourt, Canaples, Heilly, and Royon. One member fell at the siege of Damietta in 1240. Three brothers fell at Agincourt.

Another lord helped defend Paris against Joan of Arc in 1429, and won the Golden Fleece two years later. Antoine de Créquy was a bold captain under Francis the First. He died from a mishap at the siege of Hesdin in 1523. A later Antoine rose to be a cardinal. His nephew took the Créquy name and arms as heir. Charles de Blanchefort, of that line, became a marshal of France in 1622. He had married into the Lesdiguières house and inherited its title.
britannica-1911-le-chapelier-isaac-rene-:
Isaac Rene Guy Le Chapelier is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French law maker born in Rennes in seventeen fifty four. His father led the bar in that town, and the son took up the same trade. He won a name as a strong speaker in court.

The entry follows his rise when the French revolt began in seventeen eighty nine. He helped found a famed club and led the new assembly for a time. He worked on the new frame of rule and on free stage and book rights. Later he turned more mild in his views and fell under a cloud. He was seized and put to death in seventeen ninety four.
britannica-1911-le-puy:
Le Puy is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a town of south-east France. It is the capital of the Haute-Loire department of that land. The town count for 1906 is 17,291 folk. The wider commune held 21,420 folk at that count.

The town rises like a bowl's rim from 2,050 feet up. It climbs Mont Anis between two streams that meet below. Steep, narrow streets paved with lava stones lead up the hill. They reach the great church, crowned by the rock of Mont Corneille. That rock stands 433 feet above the lower town square. An iron statue of the Virgin tops the rock at its crest. It was cast from guns taken at Sebastopol in war.
britannica-1911-lefebvre-tanneguy:
Lefebvre, Tanneguy is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French classical scholar of the seventeenth century. Born at Caen in 1615 and schooled in Paris, Lefebvre, also known as Tanaquillus Faber, was made inspector of the printing press at the Louvre by Cardinal Richelieu. After the cardinal's death he left Paris, joined the Reformed Church, and in 1651 took a chair at the academy of Saumur. He filled it with great success for nearly twenty years.

Ill health and a quarrel with the church consistory, stirred in part by his mild judgment on Sappho, drove him to resign his chair. His own chief works are a set of lives of the Greek poets and a method for starting Greek and Latin studies.
britannica-1911-tuy:
Tuy, a city in the north west of Spain, fills a full place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It stands on the right bank of the Mino River, face to face with a Portuguese town. Its folk count for nineteen hundred was eleven thousand one hundred thirteen. Rail lines end here for trips to Santiago and Corunna. Rich farm land and hot springs lie in the hills near by.

Clean streets, sound homes, and many gardens mark the town in the text. Its main church was founded in the twelve hundreds and looks like a fort. Old friar houses, a bishop hall, schools, and a stage house serve the town. A fine bridge from eighteen eighty five spans the river at its feet. Past notes call it a Visigoth chief town and a fort in wars with Portugal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-le-puy:
Le Puy is a French diocese covering the whole Haute-Loire department, suffragan of Bourges. Its ancient diocese, suppressed by the 1801 Concordat and joined to Saint-Flour, rose again in 1823, taking in Brioude district as well.

Early history leans on legend: the Martyrology of Ado and St. Front's first legend tell of priest George, revived by St. Peter's staff, who founded Civitas Vetula in Velay and raised an altar to the Virgin on Mont Anis at St. Martial's request. Later traditions name Macarius, Marcellinus, Roricius, Eusebius, Paulianus, and Vosy as bishops. Vosy finished Our Lady's church and moved the see from Ruessium to Anicium. Its cathedral earned the name Angelic from angels' dedication. Duchesne warns the early chronology rests on thin evidence, with only six certain bishops before the tenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-just-hau:
René-Just Haüy, mineralogist, was born at Saint-Just in the Oise on 28 February 1743. His father was a poor weaver, and Haüy died in Paris on 3 June 1822. His early schooling came from the monks of the Premonstratensian Abbey of Saint-Just, who noticed his talent, piety, and love of church chant. Their prior sent him to Paris, where he sang as a chorister and entered the College of Navarre, later joining its teaching staff.

Ordained priest a few years later, he became Professor at the college of Cardinal Lemoine, with literature as his chosen study until a fellow professor drew him to botany. Lectures by Daubenton at the Jardin du Roi then woke a stronger interest in mineralogy, above all in the crystalline structure of minerals. He published treatises in 1803 and 1817, the latter his Traité de Cristallographie.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tuy:
Tuy is an ancient Galician city and diocese on Spain's Atlantic edge, facing Portugal across the river Minho. The entry places it within the archdiocese of Santiago, covering the civil provinces of Orense and Pontevedra. It recalls its claimed founding by the Greek hero Diomedes and its Roman past in the judicial district of Braga. Its see counts among the oldest in Spain, and its early bishops appear in records reaching back to the Visigothic age.

From its hilltop site the town moved down to the riverbank, served kings as a residence, and weathered wars along a contested border. The account names its cathedral and churches, its bishops through the centuries, and the religious houses and schools that shaped its later life. It closes with the diocese's modern bounds and clergy, giving a compact portrait of a small border see with a very long past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valentin-hauy:
Valentin Haüy founded the first school for the blind and earned the loving name Father and Apostle of the Blind. He was born at Saint-Just in Picardy on 13 November 1745 and died at Paris on 19 March 1822. He learned his first lessons with his elder brother René at the Premonstratensian abbey school near Saint-Just. Haüy never became a priest.

After his early studies he went to Paris, where he worked at calligraphy and modern languages. He taught them for a living until he joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as an interpreter of state papers. The call to teach the blind came in 1771, after he watched a burlesque show at a Paris fair that mocked blind beggars. The entry follows his school, his raised-letter books, and his pupils.
